title: Repose anchor A/B closure: fixed-nozzle pour protocol (v2)

amendment_semantics.what_changes: the POUR PROTOCOL only (nozzle height policy and burst pacing); every threshold, material micro-parameter and experimental band is inherited verbatim
amendment_semantics.reason: v1 raised the nozzle to max(drop_height, apex + 5 R) every burst, which the node report itself lists as a rejected protocol (5.3 'block-state source climbing'). Measured here: nozzle climbs to 1.44 m, the heap becomes a spire, the at-rest criterion is never met -> anchor A/B came back WITHHELD. A threshold is never relaxed to turn a WITHHELD into a PASS: the protocol is fixed, the bars stay where they were.

protocol_v2.burst_pacing: a burst is only released when the nozzle slab (drop_height - max(2.2, nozzle_clearance) R .. drop_height + 2 R + clearance) contains no sphere younger than the charge fall time; this is a physical (fall-time) pace, not a tuned number
protocol_v2.pour_closure: the pour closes when the nozzle slab is occupied by deposit at rest, or when a burst cannot place a single sphere (2.2 R exclusion); never reopened
protocol_v2.at_rest: RMS speed < 0.01 m/s sustained over 5 consecutive 100-step checks after the pour ends (inherited)
protocol_v2.calibration: single shape parameter mu_rolling fitted once on glass beads to theta_exp = 23 deg by 5-step bisection on [0.02, 0.40]; transferred unchanged to quartz sand (out of sample)
protocol_v2.measurement: heap_surface_angle (upper-envelope radial fit, 15-90 % flank window) - unchanged from v1

known_limitations_declared_up_front: the experimental bands are literature values (dry monodisperse glass beads 0.5-1.0 mm; dry rounded-to-subrounded medium quartz sand), not measured in this repository
monodisperse spheres with rolling resistance as a shape surrogate: the sand band is a shape-limited extrapolation and may honestly FAIL
n_particles = 300 is chosen for compute, not for finite-size convergence; the finite-size sensitivity is reported as a single extra run, not as a convergence study
